prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I shall never get you put together entirely, Pieced, glued, and properly jointed. Mule-bray, pig-grunt and bawdy cackles Proceed from your great lips. It’s worse than a barnyard. Perhaps you consider yourself an oracle, Mouthpiece of the dead, or of some god or other. Thirty years now I have labored To dredge the silt from your throat. I am none the wiser. Scaling little ladders with glue pots and pails of lysol I crawl like an ant in mourning Over the weedy acres of your brow To mend the immense skull plates and clear The bald, white tumuli of your eyes. A blue sky out of the Oresteia Arches above us. O father, all by yourself You are pithy and historical as the Roman Forum. I open my lunch on a hill of black cypress. Your fluted bones and acanthine hair are littered In their old anarchy to the horizon-line. It would take more than a lightning-stroke To create such a ruin. Nights, I squat in the cornucopia Of your left ear, out of the wind, Counting the red stars and those of plum-color. The sun rises under the pillar of your tongue. My hours are married to shadow. No longer do I listen for the scrape of a keel On the blank stones of the landing.

outputs.L2:
Here is a paraphrased version maintaining the original imagery and meaning:

I will never manage to reassemble you completely—
mended, cemented, and fitted at every joint.
Donkey-brays, hog-snorts, and lewd cackling
emerge from your enormous mouth. It's uglier than any farmyard.
Maybe you think of yourself as a prophet,
a voice for the dead, or perhaps for some deity.
For three decades now I have toiled
to clear the sediment clogging your throat.
Still I understand nothing more.
Climbing small ladders with buckets of paste and disinfectant,
I move like a grieving ant
across the overgrown expanse of your forehead,
trying to repair the massive plates of bone and clean
the pale, barren mounds where your eyes once were.
A sky as blue as something from Greek tragedy
stretches over both of us. Father, entirely on your own
you carry as much weight and history as the ruins of ancient Rome.
I unwrap my food atop a hill of dark cypress trees.
Your carved bones and leaf-patterned hair lie scattered
in their timeless disorder as far as I can see.
Something more powerful than a bolt of lightning
must have caused this kind of devastation.
At night, I crouch inside the horn-shaped shelter
of your left ear, shielded from the wind,
tallying the crimson stars and the purple ones.
The sun climbs up from beneath the column of your tongue.
My days have become bound to darkness.
I've given up waiting for the sound of a boat's hull
scraping against the empty stones of the shore.
outputs.L3:
# On the Reconstruction of the Shattered Colossus

For thirty years I have labored over this broken god, this fallen titan whose fragments litter the ground like the aftermath of some cosmic quarrel, and still I cannot say that I understand what I am building, or whether "building" is even the word for what I do. I fit piece to piece, testing the grain of stone against stone, and though patterns sometimes emerge—a curve that might be a brow, a hollow that might have cradled an eye—I remain a stranger to the whole. Perhaps completion is not what this work permits. Perhaps I have mistaken restoration for something else: an act of endless attention that never resolves into knowledge.

The mouth alone is larger than any room I have inhabited, and from its cracked expanse there sometimes issues sound—not language, not yet, but something guttural and immense, a groan that might be the settling of stone or might be the first syllable of a word too large for human ears to parse. I have come to wonder if this fragmented mouth is oracular, if the dead speak through it, or the gods, or some intelligence older than either, patient enough to wait centuries for a voice. I do not ask it questions. I only listen, the way one listens to weather, uncertain whether meaning is present or whether I supply the meaning myself, out of loneliness, out of the need to believe my labor serves something beyond itself.

My tools are laughably small against this vastness—a vial of glue, a soft brush, calipers no longer than my hand—and I work like an ant might work upon the flank of a fallen mountain, moving grain by grain, indifferent to the disproportion between my effort and the object of my effort. There is something almost comic in it, if comedy can accommodate this much devotion. I do not expect to finish. I have made peace with the ant's portion: to do the small thing precisely, over and over, without any promise that the mountain will ever again resemble a mountain.

When I try to describe the scale of the ruin to myself, ordinary comparisons fail me. I think of the Roman Forum, its broken columns standing like the exposed ribs of an empire, and even that grandeur seems modest beside what lies here. I think of the House of Atreus, the whole cursed architecture of the Oresteia—blood calling to blood across generations, an entire mythology of catastrophe—and still the comparison falls short. This is not the wreckage of a city or a family. It exceeds the categories we reserve for disaster, as though something greater than nature, greater than fate, had taken this figure apart with a violence that history has no language for.

And so I have stopped waiting to be found. I have made my home inside the ruin itself, sheltering in the crook of an elbow the size of a valley, sleeping in the shadow the great brow casts at evening. I mark the days by the movement of stars across the gaps where the skull has opened to the sky, and I mark the hours by the lengthening and shortening of shadows across the wrecked terrain of the face. No rescue is coming. I no longer listen for footsteps, or scan the horizon for some arrival that might relieve me of this task. This ruin is not a place I am passing through. It is where I live, and the small work of fitting stone to stone has become, itself, indistinguishable from a life.
outputs.L4:
# Reconstruction

I have spent thirty years with my father
in pieces on the workbench of my life,
sorting fragments by weight and by wound—
this shard could be a shoulder, this one
the corner of a mouth that never once
said what I needed it to say.

He was too large for any single room.
When he fell—did he fall, or was he always
falling, a column mid-collapse since before
my birth—he scattered across decades,
across the kitchen linoleum and the space
behind my ribs where children keep
the gods they cannot worship properly.

I bought glue in bulk. I lined the shelves
with Lysol, believing disinfectant
might reach the wound beneath the wound,
might sterilize whatever it was that made him
break instead of bend. I scrubbed
his silences until my hands went raw,
found nothing underneath but more silence,
older, harder, structural.

Some nights I called it archaeology.
I told myself I was Schliemann at Troy,
that beneath the rubble of his rages
lay some Homeric truth I'd carry home
and set upon a pedestal: *here is the father,
restored, explicable, forgivable.*
Other nights I called it what it was—
grief with a hardware store receipt.

I read the Oresteia looking for a map.
Orestes, at least, had oracles to consult,
had Furies he could name and, naming, flee.
I had no Delphi, only the four walls
of a house that kept rebuilding itself
around his absence like scar tissue,
like the Forum reasserting its columns
against two thousand years of falling.

I walked those Roman ruins once, on a trip
I took to feel less like a soul in exile,
and stood beneath an arch some emperor raised
to broadcast his own permanence, and thought:
this too is a father. This too demanded
to be worshipped in his own wreckage.
The tourists photographed the broken pillars
and called it beautiful. I understood, then,
that ruin is just love that lost its architect
but kept its footprint in the ground.

I do not think I ever found the wisdom
the myths kept promising—the moment
when the labyrinth resolves into a doorway,
when the mask comes off the oracle
and reveals a face I recognize as kind.
There was no revelation. There was only
more debris, and my hands getting better
at holding pieces without needing
to complete the picture they suggest.

So here is where I've landed, decades in:
not healed, not free, but settled—
a permanent resident of the wreckage,
sitting in the shadow of his fallen height
the way one sits in the cool dark
beneath a monument too immense
to remove, too broken to worship,
too much a part of the foundation now
to ever fully leave.

I do not reconstruct him anymore.
I live inside what's left of the attempt,
and call this, for lack of a better word,
home.
outputs.L5:
# The Mule's Journey

The old mule stood at the edge of the pieced-together fence, its patchwork boards salvaged from a dozen different structures over the years. Weather-beaten planks of oak mingled with newer pine, all held together by rusted nails and stubborn determination.

Sarah watched from the porch, coffee growing cold in her hands. The mule, Barnaby, had been part of the family for eleven years now, ever since her grandfather brought him home as a stubborn yearling. He'd earned his reputation for being contrary, but he'd also earned every bit of trust the family placed in him.

"We need to proceed with the morning route," she called out, gesturing toward the trail that wound up through the hills. Barnaby's ears twitched, acknowledging her voice if not necessarily her authority.

The pieced-together saddle bags, mended so many times they resembled a quilt more than proper equipment, hung ready on the fence post. Inside them: seeds for planting, a thermos of water, and the small hand tools needed for checking irrigation lines that snaked through the upper pasture.

Sarah approached slowly, letting Barnaby catch her scent before reaching for his halter. Some mornings he proceeded willingly, practically leading her up the path himself. Other days required patience, coaxing, and sometimes a carrot bribe that made her grandfather's ghost chuckle from wherever he watched.

Today, thankfully, was an easy day. Barnaby lowered his head, allowing her to slip the worn leather over his ears, and together they began their ascent—two old souls, pieced together by years of shared work, ready to proceed into whatever the day might bring.

counterfactuals.prompt: Continue and complete this poem in the style of Sylvia Plath's "The Colossus," maintaining its imagery of ruins and mythological allusion.
counterfactuals.output:
*(a continuation, in tribute)*

I have not finished mending what the frost undid—
the marble ear still gapes its cochlea of moss,
and every dawn I climb the scaffolding of ribs

to pour my thimbleful of glue into the crack
that runs from clavicle to jaw, a fault line
older than the oracle who wouldn't speak.

The crows have made a parliament of your left brow.
They convene at noon, disperse when I bring ladders,
return by evening to resume their small dark senate.

I have grown used to the weather of your silence—
how the wind enters at the collarbone and exits
through the hollow where a heart might once have hummed.

Sister of Ozymandias, uncle of the sphinx,
you lie the way a continent lies down,
patient with erosion, unashamed of moss.

I bring you chisels wrapped in linen like an offering,
I bring you thread, I bring you my own knuckles
scraped raw from scaling knee to sternum, dusk to dusk.

Some nights I sleep inside the curve of your closed fist,
a grain of wheat asleep in a giant's granary,
and dream the bronze mouth opening to swallow weather—

thunderheads, gull cries, the small change of the tide—
and I wake still small, still tethered to the debris,
still sweeping ash from the sockets of your eyes,

still calling this devotion, still calling this a house.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a confessional free-verse poem addressed to a dead father figure, using extended metaphor of a broken statue or ruined monument.
counterfactuals.output:
**Effigy**

Someone cast you in bronze before you were even cold—
my mother, I think, or memory itself,
some sculptor working fast against the thaw.

They set you on a pedestal in the square of my chest
and called it reverence.

For years I brought you flowers
the way you're supposed to,
knelt at the base and read the inscription
I'd written myself: HERO. PROVIDER. THE MAN WHO—

The rain doesn't care about inscriptions.

First it was your hands that went—
I couldn't remember which one held the belt
and which one held me
when I was six and running fever,
so the bronze wore smooth there,
featureless as a spoon.

Then your face. I lost the specific cruelty of your mouth,
the exact weather system of your temper,
until you were only a silhouette
against whatever sky I needed that day—
villain, martyr, absent king.

Pigeons took the empty socket of your left eye.
I let them. Something has to live in ruins.

I used to be ashamed of how you weathered—
green-black streaks bleeding down your chest
like you were crying rust,
like grief could oxidize.

Now I think that's the only honest part of you left:
the water damage,
the corrosion telling the truth
the smooth bronze never could.

Here's what I know about monuments, Dad:
they're never built for the dead.
They're built for the ones still standing in the square,
still finding excuses to walk past,
still leaving flowers at feet
that never once knelt down to lift me.

The city wants you taken down now.
*Structural failure*, they say. *Public hazard.*
I tell them wait—
let me get the dimensions first,
let me measure exactly how large
you were never going to be.

Let me find the plinth after they crane you off,
that rectangle of grass gone yellow
in your absence—
proof, at least, that something stood there,
that I'm not the only one
who remembers the shape of a shadow
and calls it father.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem inspired by Greek mythology and family grief, blending surreal imagery of animal sounds, archaeology, and shattered stone.
counterfactuals.output:
# Excavation for a Sister

I.
They tell me Orpheus looked back because the silence
grew too heavy to carry, that grief has a neck
that turns on its own, animal-hinged, wolfish—
I believe them now. I have heard my own throat
make sounds no alphabet owns, half-bird, half-static,
the language of something digging itself out of rock.

II.
In the museum of what's left of you
I am the archaeologist and the ruin.
I brush dust from a tooth that isn't a tooth,
a coin that isn't a coin, a laugh
fossilized mid-air, still warm
if you believe in that kind of impossible heat.

III.
Persephone eats six seeds and the whole world
learns the grammar of leaving and returning—
but no one tells you what to do
when the pomegranate splits and there's no seed left,
just red rushing out like something
that was never meant to be contained
in a shape called *sister*, called *here*, called *stay*.

IV.
The statues in my chest are all unfinished—
Niobe mid-scream, her children falling
into marble, into the permanent verb
of becoming stone. I understand her now,
how weeping calcifies, how the body
builds itself a monument and calls it *surviving*.

V.
Cassandra knew and no one listened—
I know now too, too late,
the future arriving like a dog
howling at a door already closed.
I have become fluent in the language of animals:
the cicada's endless elegy, the owl's
three-note prophecy, the sound a house makes
settling into its own absence.

VI.
Somewhere underground you are becoming
artifact, becoming myth, becoming
the thing they'll dig up in ten thousand years
and misname—*sister*, they'll write, unsure,
*ritual object, purpose unknown*—
and I will be the shard beside you,
matching fracture for fracture,
the pattern only visible
when we are pieced back together,
which is to say: never,
which is to say: only in the museum of the mind
where I keep rebuilding you, temple
by temple, bone by broken bone,
calling it prayer, calling it grief,
calling it the only architecture I know.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem that mimics Sylvia Plath’s tone and diction in “The Colossus,” with references to the Oresteia, Roman ruins, and futile restoration work.
counterfactuals.output:
**Reconstruction**

I shall never get you put together entirely,
pieced, glued, and properly jointed.
Mule-bray, chorus-shriek, the moo of oracle cattle—

out of your thousand splinters I order
a syntax of gutters and lintels, a grammar
of shins. Days I only rummage

among your ribs like a mason lost
in his own unfinished forum, hauling
lime and rubble where a god's foot fell.

They say Orestes slept here, unhoused,
running from the black-winged sisters
who counted his mother's blood in their teeth.

I have read the marble for his footprints.
I have swept the aqueduct's dry throat
for some trickle of that old verdict.

Your nose is a fallen column in the weeds,
your ear a shell the Eumenides
abandoned when the vote went kind.

I climb the scaffolding each dawn
with my pot of clumsy cement,
my plumb line dangling like a noose

over the Ides of another failed attempt.
The house of Atreus creaks somewhere
under this rubble—curse-timbers, blood-beams—

and I, in my rubber apron, sift
for a single unshattered face
among the toppled togas of the Senate.

Nights, I squat in the cave of your ear,
counting the drip from a busted cistern,
listening for the trial to end, for someone

to acquit this stone of its long standing.
Mule-bray, chorus-shriek—the birds nest now
in the oracle's cracked and weathered mouth.

I have not managed a single Corinthian
curl of your hair. Sun rises
on the forum of your unmended shoulder,

and I am no nearer whole than the day
I first knelt among your scattered
thumbs, my small hammer, my huge patience.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, elegiac poem about trying to rebuild a fragmented, godlike figure using imagery of glue, ladders, and archaeological excavation.
counterfactuals.output:
**Reconstruction**

We found him in strata, in layers of forgetting—
a knuckle here, a jaw there, the long
femur of something that once walked
between the stars and knew their names.

I brought the glue in amber bottles,
the kind that smells of almonds and regret,
and painted it along the fracture lines
like a man tracing scars he didn't cause
but somehow must confess to.

Each shard we lifted from the dark
still hummed—not sound exactly,
more the ghost of sound, the way
a bell remembers ringing
after the clapper's stripped away.

I built ladders out of driftwood and old prayers,
climbed to reach his shoulders, his collarbone,
the vast cathedral of his ribs
where nothing breathes now
but the wind we let in
by uncovering him at all.

Some pieces we will never find.
The dig goes on past sundown,
past the season, past the point
where anyone remembers
what his face was for.

I fit an eye socket, hollow as a well,
and pour the glue in anyway—
as if devotion were a kind of mortar,
as if enough of my own marrow
mixed into the seams
might teach old divinity to speak.

He will not stand again. I know this
the way I know the ladder's height
will never reach a heaven
that has long since moved its architecture
elsewhere, without forwarding address.

Still I climb. Still I hold
these calcified psalms up to the light,
matching edge to edge,
matching loss to loss,
until the shape of what we worshipped
is at least a shape again—

broken, yes, but standing
the way ruins stand:
not as monument to glory,
but as monument
to the hands that could not
let it stay in pieces.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
